sections.body:
Competence shaming is a way of raising your own standing by lowering somebody else's. The speaker shows the room that another person cannot do the work, and the room takes the speaker to be the one who can. The material is often real. The error is the handle, not the point.

Two different things happen when somebody criticises work. One is **disagreement with the work**: the reader is told what is wrong, so that it can be made right. The other is an attack on the person behind the work: the reader is told what is wrong, so that the person is made smaller. The words can be identical. *"The number in table two is wrong"* can be the first or the second, and the sentence itself will not tell you which.

Status is the place a person holds in a group: the respect, the authority and the trust that the others give them. Every group has a ranking, and the ranking is worked on in every meeting. **Credibility** is the part of status that says *this person's word about their own work can be trusted*. A status attack spends the other person's credibility to buy the speaker's.

Honest criticism is a gift, and the gift is not rare. It names the defect, it tells the person what to do, and it leaves their standing intact — often it makes the standing stronger, because the person who fixed the problem in front of everybody is now known to be careful. Competence shaming uses the same facts and spends them in the other direction. So the test is not *was the criticism true?* It is *what happens to the work, and to the person, if this lands?*
examples: The number in table two is wrong — the corrected value is on the sheet.
That was about the work, so it made the work better.
It was not about the report. It was about making the other person smaller.
sections.heading: What competence shaming is

terms.example: It was competence shaming: a real error became the reason to put her down in front of the team.
terms.gloss: Raising your own standing by showing that another person cannot do the work.

terms.example: Her status in the room changed the moment she was corrected in front of the client.
terms.gloss: The place a person holds in a group: the respect and the authority that other people give them.

terms.example: A public correction took her credibility away, and it took months to get it back.
terms.gloss: The part of a person's standing that says their word about their own work can be trusted.

sections.body:
The public correction. The correction itself is not the attack. The setting is. The same sentence said in the corridor and said in the review meeting does two different things. A **public correction** lands in front of the people whose respect the speaker wants. Its work is not only to correct the work: it is to make the corrected person visibly smaller, in the sight of the people whose judgement will decide the next promotion. Watch where it happens, and who is sitting there.

The hedge that never resolves. Sometimes there is no open correction at all. The speaker says *"I am not sure the numbers are right"* — and then nothing. A second doubt arrives, and a third. The work is never confirmed and the doubt is never closed. This is **hedging**: saying that something may be wrong without ever saying what is right. In a meeting it sounds careful. Its function is to keep the other person's standing unresolved, and an unresolved standing is worth less than a lowered one.

The test of competence in front of an audience. *"Let me ask you to explain the whole procedure to the team."* Now the speaker has built a small stage: the other person has to perform, and the room is watching. The subject of the question is beside the point. What matters is who looks fluent in front of the room and who does not. The **audience** is part of the move, because without a witness there is no ranking to shift. The move is also cheap: the cost lands on the person who cannot answer quickly, and not at all on the person who asked.

The compliment that carries the insult. *"Good job catching that — you are very careful."* The praise is not about the work. It is about the failure, and it hands the room a picture of the person as the one who makes the mistakes. This is **devaluation** wearing good manners: the value that other people attach to the person's judgement is lowered while everybody is being friendly. It is also the hardest move to refuse, because there is nothing in the compliment to object to.
examples: The correction happened in the review, in front of the whole team.
I am not sure the numbers are right — I will leave it open for now.
Let me ask you to explain the whole procedure to the team.
Good job catching that. You are very careful.
sections.heading: The four moves of the attack

terms.example: The public correction in the review meeting lasted a minute and stayed with her for a month.
terms.gloss: A correction of somebody's work made in front of other people, where the correction also lowers their standing.

terms.example: The hedging ran for weeks: doubt after doubt, and never one confirmed number.
terms.gloss: Saying that something may be wrong without ever saying what is right, so that the doubt stays open.

terms.example: Without an audience there is no ranking to shift, so the question stayed in the corridor.
terms.gloss: The people who are present and watching; in a status attack the audience is what makes the move cheap.

terms.example: The devaluation was quiet: every meeting began with a small doubt about her work.
terms.gloss: The act of lowering the value that other people attach to a person's work or judgement.

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in a workplace document, in a report written after a conflict, and in the ordinary English of a team. Learn them because you need the name in order to write the sentence, and because a feeling that has no name stays a feeling.

Status maintenance is the work a person does to keep their place in a group: preparing, presenting, and being seen to know more than the next person. Maintenance needs fuel, and it also means that a person who is losing standing will look for a way to lower somebody else. The ranking has to be defended, and the cheapest defence is somebody else's mistake.

Undermining is the slow work of taking away a person's confidence in their own judgement: *"are you sure?"*, *"that is a bold choice"*, *"I am only asking"*. Each remark is small. Repeated, they take the ground from under the person, who starts to check their work three times and then apologises for the work that was right. Undermining is the slow cousin of the public correction, and it leaves no sentence to point at afterwards.

Saving face is the practice of letting a person keep their standing, especially after a mistake. A good correction saves face: it names the defect, it does not stage the person who made it, and it lets the work move on. **Professional face** is the public standing a person carries at work — the regard of colleagues, clients and the team. It is a real thing with real consequences: a person whose professional face has been damaged will be treated differently, whatever the truth of the criticism.
examples: Status maintenance is why she read the report twice before she sent it.
Are you sure? It is only a question.
He let me correct the figure without naming who had written it.
After the review, her professional face was in pieces for a month.
sections.heading: The words the field uses

terms.example: Status maintenance is why she read the report twice before she sent it.
terms.gloss: The work a person does to keep their place and their standing in a group.

terms.example: The undermining was a few small remarks spread over a month, and none of them alone was worth arguing with.
terms.gloss: The slow, repeated work of taking away a person's confidence in their own judgement.

terms.example: The manager saved face by letting the report be corrected without naming who had written it.
terms.gloss: Letting a person keep their standing, especially after a mistake or a failure.

terms.example: His professional face was in pieces for a month after the review.
terms.gloss: The public standing a person carries at work: the regard of colleagues, clients and the team.

sections.body:
Two columns and one test. The left column is the criticism you want. The right column is the attack. The content may be the same in both; what differs is the question behind the words, and what happens next.

Read the rows in order: the question, then the place, then the effect on the work, then the effect on the person. The last two rows carry most of the signal. A correction that never reaches the work is not criticism, whatever anybody calls it.

One incident is not a pattern. A senior engineer may correct a junior in public for one good reason. The pattern is what repeats: the same person, the same kind of remark, the same effect on the same colleague. Judge the pattern and the aim, and keep the pattern separate from the person.
examples: What is wrong with this, and how do I fix it?
The question was who cannot do this, not what is wrong with the work.
One correction in public is not a pattern. The same remark every week is.
sections.heading: Honest criticism and a status attack, side by side

rows: What is wrong with this, and how do I fix it?
Who here is not able to do this?
In the room where the work is done: a check, a pair working on it, a review with the owner there.
In front of the people whose respect matters, at the moment the speaker gains from it.
What it does to the work
The defect is named, the fix is named, the work is corrected and moves on.
The defect becomes a story about a person, and the work stops being the subject of the meeting.
What it does to the person
The standing is untouched, and often it grows: the person is known to be somebody who fixes things.
The person is smaller in the room, and the doubt stays open afterwards.
What happens if you refuse it
Nothing. The work is still discussed, because the work is what was being discussed.
The refusal is treated as one more failure, in front of the same people.

sections.body:
Six steps. They take under a minute, they need no authority you do not have, and they do not require you to decide what anybody meant. The aim is to protect the work and your standing, not to win the exchange.

The first three steps keep the exchange on the work. The last three keep you out of the ranking the other person is trying to build. None of them accuses anybody, and none of them needs the room on your side.

The hardest step is the first one, because the room is waiting for you to defend yourself, and defending yourself is what moves the subject from the work to the person.
examples: The number in table two is wrong; the corrected value is on the sheet.
What would the correct version look like?
Your question was about the drawing. Let me answer that first.
sections.heading: How to answer a status attack without escalating
steps: Move the question to the work. Name the defect and the fix in one sentence: "The number in table two is wrong; the corrected value is on the sheet." Say nothing about the person.
Ask what the fix is. If the criticism is vague, ask for the shape of the correct version: "What would the correct version look like?" The question is hard to answer when the aim was never the work.
Close the item in writing. Send a short note with the corrected item and what changed. A written closure gives an open doubt an end, and it keeps the same record for both sides.
Do not answer the attack with an attack. A status attack answered in the same register gives the room the ranking it was built for. Keep your voice on the work.
Name the deflection and answer the question that was asked. If the answer turns into a question about you, answer the original question first, then answer the new one in a single sentence.

Move the rest to writing and keep a short record. Write down the date, the words that were used, and who said them. If the pattern continues, this record is what you will need in the next conversation.

terms.example: The deflection worked once, and I still had not answered what was wrong with the drawing.
terms.gloss: Turning a question back on the person who asked it, so that the original question is never answered.

sections.body:
It does not settle every disagreement into an attack. Two people can disagree about the same document and both be honest. The word *status* is not a verdict on a person, and reading it into an ordinary correction damages a working relationship for nothing.

It does not give a licence to call every boss a manipulator. A manager who corrects you in front of a client may be doing it badly. A manager who does it because it works is doing it deliberately, and the difference shows in what happens after the correction, not in the correction itself. This article gives you the test and the sentences; the judgement is still yours to make.

And it does not replace the ordinary channels. A repeated pattern of public correction is a matter for the code of conduct, for the manager above, for the HR file, or for the law — not only for a good sentence. Use the sentences to protect the work in the room, and use the channels when the pattern continues.

One last limit. This article describes the move from the outside, and from the outside you can see the words and the setting, not the intention. When you can see only those, the honest answer is *I do not know which one this was* — and you can still ask the useful question: what is wrong with the work, and how do I fix it?
examples: Two people can disagree about a document, and both of them can be right.
The pattern is a matter for the code of conduct, not only for a good sentence.
I do not know which one this was, so I will ask about the work.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
The first group is for the meeting. It keeps the sentence on the work, and it is the sentence to use when the room is waiting for you to defend yourself.

The second group is for the review and for the written note. It closes the item, so that the doubt has an end and the record is the same for everybody.

The third group is for the moment when the subject turns to you. Keep it short, keep it on the record, and do not pay the compliment back.
examples: The number in table two is wrong; the corrected value is on the sheet.
What would the correct version look like?
Let us keep this on the drawing, not on the person.
I am happy to be corrected. I would like to know the fix.
Here is the item, corrected, and here is what changed.
Closing the item: the figure is 12.4 now, and the note is updated.
Your question was about the drawing. Let me answer that first.
I would like to take this one to writing, so that we both have the same record.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
In a group the move is cheaper, and the reason is structural. A status attack needs two things: a person to put down, and a witness who will make the ranking visible. A group supplies both without asking. Every meeting is a chance to reorder the room, and the reordering costs the person who does it nothing.

The audience also protects the attacker. A private correction can be answered in private. A public one has to be answered in public, in the moment, in front of the same people. The pressure of the moment does the work of the argument: the corrected person either takes it and looks small, or answers and looks defensive. Both outcomes serve the person who spoke.

So a group learns the move as soon as the group rewards it. When the person who wins the room by lowering somebody else is praised, promoted or left alone, the group learns that this is how a place is taken. **Subordination** — the arrangement in which one person is placed below another and kept there — stops being a description of the hierarchy and becomes a method for holding it. An organisation that rewards the move will keep producing it, and it will call it a leadership style.

What stops it is ordinary and works: the norm that criticism is about the work. A team where the correction happens in private, or where the person who corrects also says what the fix is, keeps the ranking out of the argument. And a team where several people are willing to say *"that is about the person, not the work"* keeps the check alive, because one person who always says it will be stopped.
examples: The ranking was rearranged in the room, and nobody voted for it.
The pressure of the moment did the work of the argument.
That is about the person, not the work.
sections.heading: The same move in a group

terms.example: The subordination was taught in the meeting: whoever spoke second was corrected first.
terms.gloss: The arrangement in which one person is placed below another and kept there.

item.summary: Competence shaming is a way of gaining standing by lowering somebody else's competence, and the difference from honest criticism is the aim, not the words. After reading this you can name the four moves of the attack, tell honest criticism from a status attack, answer one without escalating it, and notice when you are doing it yourself.
item.title: Competence Shaming and Status Manipulation
